newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK unemployment shows sharpest fall on record.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK unemployment shows sharpest fall on record.

text.p: Unemployment in Britain plunged by nearly 96,000 -- the largest fall on record -- to below the psychologically important two million level in November, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Wednesday.

The ONS also published robust retail sales figures for November which provided further evidence of vigorous economic growth, increasing pressure on the Conservative government to raise interest rates before a general election due by next May.
Unemployment fell in November by 95,800 to 1.929 million, adjusted for seasonal variations, the first figure below two million since early 1991.
Commenting on the figures during a visit to Northern Ireland, Prime Minister John Major said: "They are not good, they are magnificent."
"What we can see as we come to Christmas 1996 are perhaps the best economic prospects that we have seen across the United Kingdom for a very long time," he added.

However, City of London economists said the jobs and high street sales figures would make it harder for the government to resist Bank of England pressure to raise interest rates from the present 6.0 percent to choke off inflationary pressures.

The Conservatives, who lost their overall majority in parliament after a by-election defeat last week, are anxious to avoid raising interest rates again before the election as this would mean dearer home loans for millions of people.

The opposition Labour party, which is well ahead of the Conservatives in opinion polls, poured scorn on the jobless figures, saying they could only be explained by people being driven off the unemployment register.
"No-one believes their bogus figures. More people believe in Santa Claus," said Labour's deputy leader John Prescott.

The dramatic drop in unemployment was partly due to the introduction of a new "jobseekers' allowance" and changes in rules on means-testing for benefits. These two factors accounted for a drop of around 25,000 in the jobless count.
That still left a drop of around 70,000 in the underlying figure, nearly three times what the markets were expecting.
Education and employment secretary Gillian Shephard said unemployment should not be expected to continue falling at the same pace. "We cannot expect falls of this size every month," she said.
Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets, said that while the figures showed the labour market was tightening, wage growth remained encouragingly moderate.
"There is little evidence that this is causing upward pressure on wages, with underlying average earnings sticking at a moderate four percent for the fourth month running in October," he said.
This view was shared by the Confederation of British Industry, Britain's leading business organisation.
"The fact that this sharp fall in unemployment has not yet resulted in any increase in earnings growth is extremely encouraging," it said.
Retail sales were up 0.7 percent in November from the previous month, giving an annual growth rate of 3.9 percent.
Average earnings figures for October, also published on Wednesday, showed no change from the September figure of 4.0 percent.
Unit wage costs eased slightly to an annual growth rate of 4.6 percent in the three months to October from 4.7 percent in the three months to September.
